newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria Socialists choose PM, opposition protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Socialists choose PM, opposition protests.

text.p: Protesters threw snowballs and stale loaves at the offices of Bulgaria's ruling Socialists on Wednesday as their coalition allies approved strongman interior minister Nikolai Dobrev as the country's new premier.
The opposition wants new elections, says the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) has failed to tackle the economic crisis and no longer has enough support to form a government.

"The protesters are right. Incomes have fallen and life has become even more difficult. The BSP's rule so far is to be blamed for all this," Dobrev told a news conference. "I will try not to make the mistakes of the previous governments."

More than 20,000 protesters carrying broomsticks with signs saying "We'll clean you out of the country" and "We want to live without you" surrounded the party headquarters. Some threw flowers and firecrackers at riot police guarding the building.

"We protest against communist rulers who do not want to give their people a chance. The only thing they fight for is to remain in power for one day, week or month longer," said Ivan Kostov, leader of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces.

Thousands marched in parallel protests in two other big towns. The UDF has scheduled more rallies on Thursday and Friday, emulating demonstrations against the Socialist government in neighbouring Yugoslavia.

Dobrev's government will be Bulgaria's ninth since the end of one-party rule in 1989. Prime Minister Zhan Videnov resigned at a party congress last month after months of criticism of his handling of the economy.
"I will be ready to discuss with all political forces the problems of the economy and social order," Dobrev said. "I plan to carry out radical reform which will boost economic growth."
Dobrev, 49, emerged as an outspoken critic of Videnov at the congress, attacking the cabinet's record and raising the previously taboo issue of government corruption.
Critics of his candidature say he lacks the economic background and international contacts necessary to win the approval of Bulgaria's foreign partners.
Dobrev became interior minister last May after his predecessor Lyubomir Nachev was dismissed for failing to deal with escalating crime.
He has also been BSP organisational secretary dealing with human resources issues and has chaired parliament's national security committee.

He is seen as one of the party's strongmen due to the access to information provided by his posts. Bulgarian police files from the communist era have never been made public as they were in East Germany.
Analysts said some deputies might not welcome a figure who could crack down on attempts to use public power for private interests.
President Zhelyu Zhelev is expected to give Dobrev a mandate to form a cabinet on Friday and ask parliament within seven days to approve his nomination and vote on the cabinet.
The Socialists plan to discuss the new cabinet at a plenum on Sunday. Some ministers are expected to retain their posts.
One of the first tasks of Dobrev's government will be to negotiate with multilateral lenders implementation of a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime to restore confidence in the national currency.
It might also withdraw the 1997 budget bill approved by the outgoing cabinet last week and propose a new one.
